summary: Describes how link-layer status information from various access technologies, such as link up and down events, can help IP quickly detect that a host has attached to a different network. It gives a non-exhaustive catalogue of what well-known technologies can provide. It is informational.

eli5.summary: When your wifi connects or drops, the network card knows first. This lists how it can quickly tell the rest of the computer.

questions: how does ip detect network attachment changes
how does device detect network change
subtitle: How network interfaces signal when they connect or disconnect.

tldr.problem: When a device moves between networks, IP needs to detect this quickly to update its configuration. But network-layer indications may not arrive immediately.
tldr.mechanism: Link-layer events, especially link up notifications, can signal to the IP layer when a physical connection is established or changes, enabling faster detection of network movement.
tldr.outcome: Different access technologies (cellular, WiFi, Ethernet) provide different types and timing of link-layer events, giving IP a catalogue of what to expect.

today: RFC 4957 is an Informational document describing how different access technologies signal network attachment events. It provides guidance to DNA specifications but does not define or mandate any specific behavior. The catalogue of link-layer events it describes remains current for the technologies listed, though newer wireless standards (such as LTE and 5G) and link discovery mechanisms may provide additional or different signals.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Devices that move between networks, whether mobile phones switching base stations or laptops joining different WiFi networks, need to detect when their network attachment point has changed. Often this means the IP subnet has changed too, requiring updates to IP addresses, gateways, and DNS servers.

The link layer (the lowest layer handling physical connection) detects these changes before the IP layer does. Link-layer event notifications can alert IP quickly that a network attachment has changed, prompting it to probe for new configuration. Without such notifications, IP must wait for router advertisements, unreachability timeouts, or other slow indications.

This document catalogues what link-layer notifications different well-known access technologies can provide, to guide design of systems that detect network attachment changes (a process called DNA, for Detecting Network Attachment).
sections.eli5: When your device connects to a new network, the network card knows instantly. The card can send a signal saying it is connected or disconnected, and this signal helps the computer figure out its new network address quickly.

sections.title: Terminology and Concepts
sections.content:
A link is the physical communication medium between nodes, such as a cable, radio channel, or switch port. The attachment point is the endpoint where a device connects, such as an access point (WiFi), base station (cellular), or switch port (Ethernet).

A link up event is the most useful signal for detecting network attachment. It occurs when the link layer successfully establishes a connection and is ready to pass IP packets. The link layer generates this event after its own protocols complete, such as association in WiFi or context activation in cellular networks. By the time the notification reaches IP, the link is ready to send and receive data.

Link-layer notifications may carry auxiliary information along with the event, such as the identity of the attachment point (a WiFi SSID or base station ID) or IP-layer configuration parameters obtained during connection (such as an IPv4 address). This extra information helps IP decide whether the subnet has actually changed, since moving to a different access point may not always mean moving to a different subnet.
sections.eli5: When the connection succeeds, the network card sends a 'link up' message. This message might include the network's name or the IP address to use, helping the computer figure out where it is.

sections.title: Link-Layer Events in Common Technologies
sections.content:
Different technologies provide different levels of event notification. Cellular networks (GPRS/3GPP and cdma2000/3GPP2) generate a clear link up event when a packet data connection is activated. For GPRS, this is when a PDP Context is established; for cdma2000, it is when the Point-to-Point Protocol (PPP) reaches its opened state. Both can carry an IPv4 address as auxiliary information.

WiFi (IEEE 802.11) generates link up events upon successful association or re-association with an access point, or after completing a security handshake in networks using WPA or WPA2. The notification can include the BSSID (the unique ID of the access point) and SSID (the network name). However, these identifiers do not reliably indicate whether the IP subnet has changed, since an access point may connect to multiple subnets and the same network name may be used by different operators.

Ethernet (IEEE 802.3) presents the most complex case. Link Integrity Tests at the physical layer report when the medium is ready for frames. However, in switched networks using Spanning Tree Protocol (STP), the switch may block a port to prevent loops even after the link appears ready. Hosts cannot easily know when the switch has finished STP calculations. The RFC suggests listening to STP and 802.1AB Link-Layer Discovery Protocol (LLDP) messages to refine the link status, or waiting for a 20-second bridge timeout.
sections.eli5: Phones tell the network instantly when they are connected. WiFi networks send the network name. Ethernet is trickier because switches need to think about loops, so the computer might not know it is really ready to send yet.

sections.title: Security Implications
sections.content:
Link-layer events can be spoofed or manipulated by attackers. An attacker could send fake link up events to move a device away from a legitimate network, or send false information about the attachment point. In WiFi, the 'Evil Twin' attack creates an access point with the same name as a legitimate one, deceiving users.

This RFC does not provide protection mechanisms. Instead, it recommends relying on security in other layers. For example, IEEE 802.1ae (MAC Security) provides authentication and integrity protection for Ethernet management frames. At the IP layer, SEND (Secure Neighbor Discovery, RFC 3971) can verify reachability with a router. However, no network-layer mechanism can protect against all link-layer spoofing, especially attacks that make the physical link non-functional.
sections.eli5: Bad actors can fake these signals to trick your device. Better security at other layers, like checking that the router is really who it says it is, can help.

sections.title: Why This Matters
sections.content:
Fast detection of network attachment changes enables better mobility support. Without link-layer events, mobile IP handovers are slow and involve re-routable prefixes and tunnels. With link-layer hints, devices can immediately probe for new addresses, reducing the time spent without connectivity during a handoff.

The document emphasizes that a link up event does not always mean a subnet change. For example, a device moving between WiFi access points on the same network should not trigger IP reconfiguration. The DNA process must use link-layer events as a signal to investigate further, not as definitive proof of subnet change.

This catalogue helps specifications for DNA (in both IPv4 and IPv6) understand what indications to expect from real networks, so they can design robust detection mechanisms that work across diverse technologies.
sections.eli5: This helps devices move between networks without losing connection. It is informational, meaning it does not set rules, just describes what different network technologies already do.
